bib.title: Natural Language Processing with Python, Chapter 10: Analyzing the Meaning of Sentences
bib.venue: O'Reilly Media (book chapter; year inferred from the O'Reilly NLTK book, not printed in the chapter text)

question: How can a sentence's meaning be represented so that a program can answer questions, check consistency and resolve scope and anaphora?
contributions: Translates English questions into SQL by building a SEM feature value alongside the parse, as a first case of meaning representation
Introduces propositional and first-order logic, models, valuations and assignments, with Prover9 for proofs and Mace4 for countermodels
Builds sentence meanings compositionally with the lambda-calculus, treats quantifier scope ambiguity with Cooper storage, and extends to discourse with DRT

results.claim: A feature grammar with SEM values built by string concatenation turns 'What cities are located in China' into SELECT City FROM city_table WHERE Country="china".
results.setup: sql0.fcfg grammar and NLTK load_parser over the Chat-80 city table
results.quote: SELECT City FROM city_table WHERE Country="china"

results.claim: The Chat-80 city table gives Athens a population of 1368 (thousands); the data date from at least the 1980s.

Mace4 builds a countermodel for premises 'a woman every man loves; Adam is a man; Eve is a woman' with conclusion 'Adam loves Eve': Adam and Eve denote the same individual a in the model, and the woman every man loves is a second individual b.
results.setup: nltk.MaceCommand over a4, a5, a6; valuation printed with Skolem constant C1
results.quote: Mace4 found a countermodel in which there is some woman other
results.note: Shows the premises leave background knowledge (that Adam loves Eve) unstated; adding a premise rules the countermodel out.

results.claim: 'Everybody admires someone' has two first-order readings: all x.(person(x) -> exists y...) allows a different admired person per x, while exists y.(... all x ...) requires a single admired person.

A syntax-driven translation always gives the first scoping, e.g. 'Every girl chases a dog' becomes all x.(girl(x) -> exists y.(dog(y) & chase(x,y))) and never the reversed scope; Cooper storage generates every ordering.
results.quote: will always be translated as (53a), not (53b)

results.claim: A discourse representation structure holds discourse referents and conditions, so the quantifier in 'Angus owns a dog' binds the pronoun in 'It bit Irene' across two sentences.
results.quote: Angus owns a dog. It bit Irene.

limits: The SQL grammar is hand-written for one table and a few words; the chapter itself says the restricted-domain approach does not generalize without a theory of meaning.
Logic-based semantics handles consistency and entailment but not lexical meaning, vagueness or world knowledge; Mace4 countermodels expose missing premises rather than supply them.
No evaluation on a benchmark: all results are worked examples with toy models.
Code uses Python 2 and NLTK 2 APIs; Prover9 and Mace4 are external binaries.
practices: Check a meaning representation by evaluating it in a model and by asking a prover for entailment, and ask a model builder for a countermodel when a proof fails (10.3).
Make scope ambiguity explicit by generating all scopings (Cooper storage) instead of accepting the one the parse tree yields (10.4).
Keep a running discourse structure so that pronouns resolve to discourse referents introduced earlier (10.5).

terms.definition: a grammar feature whose value is a meaning representation built from the children's values during parsing
a formal representation of a situation as a domain of individuals and sets built from it, in which given sentences are true
a mapping from constants and predicates to their denotations in a model
a notation that abstracts over variables so that meanings of parts compose by function application and beta-reduction
a method that stores quantifiers with a semantic representation and retrieves them in any order to produce all scopings
a list of discourse referents plus conditions, used to represent the meaning of a multi-sentence discourse
